title: FIA confirms unanimous agreement on 2030 PU framework
excerpt:
The FIA has announced that a unanimous agreement has been reached on the 2030 power unit technical framework among the governing body, Formula 1, teams and power unit manufacturers.

Prioritising sustainable technology and limited hybridisation, the framework proposes a 2.1-litre turbocharged V8 that will run on sustainable fuels and be more cost-effective for teams.

This change would mark the first appearance of V8s since the 2013 season and is intended to encourage closer, more attacking racing that enhances the sporting spectacle for fans around the world.

In addition to the reintroduction of the engine’s distinctive sound, the FIA announced that "the plan is to marry the V8 power unit to a chassis which will also be lighter, more agile and placing greater emphasis on driver skill and close racing".

The next stage is to present a definitive 2030 Regulatory Framework to the FIA World Motor Sport Council meeting in Shanghai next month, as all regulatory changes are subject to approval.

Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, said: “This agreement marks a significant milestone in shaping the future of Formula 1. From the outset I have been clear in my ambition to deliver a sport that is more competitive and more exciting for our fans, while remaining at the forefront of innovation and sustainability.

“The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this Championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide. Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition.

“I want to thank all involved for their collaboration. This is an important step forward, and demonstrates what we can achieve when we work together to deliver the best possible future for our sport.”

title: Cadillac CEO Towriss on Herta’s future and Bottas’ extension
excerpt:
Cadillac CEO Dan Towriss has given an update on Colton Herta’s future after the American missed out on a potential F1 promotion in 2027, following the announcement that Valtteri Bottas will remain with the squad.

While Sergio Perez’s contract extension was confirmed ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix in October, speculation persisted over whether Bottas would stay in the other seat or if Herta – who has acted as a test driver for the team this year – might be given the opportunity.

Alongside embarking on his debut F2 campaign in 2026, Herta has participated in six Free Practice 1 outings for Cadillac – meaning that he accumulated enough Super Licence points to allow him to race in F1.

However, the American outfit ultimately decided to retain Bottas for 2027, a decision that Towriss reiterated was “right” for them as he spoke to the media on Thursday at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

When asked if there was ever any doubt over Bottas’ position, Towriss responded: “We did want to take a look at it. I think as we look across the races, while [his pace in] practice and Qualifying was similar to Checo, race pace was down.

“Some of that [involves] things behind the scenes that are out of Valtteri's control. We did want to take a look at that. We were working hard to get Colton Herta ready as well.

“It's important to have an American driver for our team with our team, racing, but ultimately, when we took a look at it, Valtteri's the right guy.

“We want to keep Checo and Valtteri together, their experience, the continuity, what they bring to the team. Ultimately it was the right decision for the team and we were happy to extend Valtteri. He's been absolutely fantastic for us.”

In terms of what this means for Herta’s next steps, Towriss explained that there are “a number of options on the table” for the 26-year-old.

“We've offered him a reserve position,” the American said. “The seat's open for ’28, so there are options on the table for Colton. There are options in other sports as well. I think he's decided on a direction, but we're still in conversations on that and look forward to seeing what Colton wants to do.”

Towriss acknowledged that Herta was “disappointed” by the decision and went on to praise the former IndyCar racer for taking on the challenge of the past year.

“It was definitely a tough decision – a tough discussion with Colton,” he explained. “I think he was disappointed. There was a lot of work, a lot of a build-up [to] go into this. I know Colton was very brave in even taking on this risk, going into F2 and trying to cram all this learning in.

“I think it was obvious it was a very tough season for Colton in F2 this year, but I think the work that he did in FP1s and the TPC [Testing of Previous Cars] setting [was] quite strong and showed that he really is capable of driving this car. But when we look at where the team is right now and what's needed for the team, Valtteri was the best decision going forward.

“But we're going to continue to talk to Colton about the options that are on the table and give it a little bit of time, because I think he is disappointed to not have that opportunity. So much went into this, but he's just a tremendous talent and we're excited about what's ahead for him.”

title: Aron leaves Alpine as Vesti doubles up in reserve role
excerpt:
Alpine have confirmed that reserve driver Paul Aron has been released from his duties by mutual agreement.

For the last three races of the season his role will be filled by Mercedes reserve Fred Vesti, who will double up across the two teams.

Aron has reportedly opted for a return to the Formula E series, having previously competed in two races in the category in the 2023-24 season, while he also tested for the new Fortescue team in Jarama.

Aron had high hopes of becoming Estonia’s first F1 driver. A former Mercedes junior, he finished third in FIA F3 in 2023 and in FIA F2 the following year.

Those performances propelled him into the F1 reserve role with Alpine after a good showing in the 2024 Abu Dhabi rookie test.

Over the past two seasons he has completed five FP1 session with Alpine, while unusually he was also loaned out to Sauber/Audi, running a further four sessions for the Hinwil outfit.

However, there was no clear progression to a race seat at either team, and with Freddie Slater now firmly in the reserve role at Audi and Gabriele Mini impressing on his two recent FP1 outings with Alpine – including a P7 in Brazil – Aron’s chances appeared to be receding.

After two seasons on the sidelines, like others who have found themselves in similar situations, he was keen to move on and find a race seat somewhere.

"Paul hasn't raced for two years,” said Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen. “He's been our reserve and done a great job in the sim, and his reserve duties. But he wanted to go back to racing, so he's chosen his path, and we're happy to let him go and wish him luck for the future.”

While Vesti is filling the Alpine reserve role for the remainder of the season, Nielsen wouldn’t be drawn on who might get the job in 2027, although Mini would be a logical choice.

"Not sure beyond that,” he said. “No firm plans. We're looking at various alternatives, but Fred's in for the last three races as a reserve, and we’re happy to have his services.”

title: What the teams said – Thursday in Las Vegas
excerpt:
The drivers and teams report back from the first two practice sessions at the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend.

Nov 20, 2026 10:59am UTC

Mercedes

Kimi Antonelli is running with the upgraded turbocharger here, but his team mate is not. As such, Mercedes sent the Italian out first in FP1 to sample the conditions, before George Russell came out for one lap late on. It was then revealed that Antonelli was running a new ICE as well, meaning he has a five-place grid drop incoming for Saturday’s Grand Prix.

In the second session, both drivers were keen to get some laps in on the wet tyres and then the inters. Russell wound up topping the session courtesy of a very late lap on the intermediate tyres, with Antonelli winding up a little down the order after setting his time much earlier.

Kimi Antonelli - FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:49.043, P8

"It was a strange day with the weather meaning we didn’t get any real running in FP1 and no real representative running in FP2. It wasn’t the easiest day therefore to build a rhythm. We still managed to learn a few things though and we have some things to look through overnight. We weren’t as competitive as we would have liked on the Intermediate tyre so that will be useful to explore, even if it isn’t learning that we will need for the rest of the weekend here in Las Vegas.

"Tomorrow should be a very different day if it stays dry, and FP3 will therefore be important. We’ll need to maximise the running, get comfortable with the car in those conditions and understand the tyres, particularly with the limited information everyone has from today. I’m feeling positive though. The car has been performing well recently and hopefully we can have a productive final practice and put ourselves in a good position for qualifying."

George Russell - FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:47.272, P1

"It’s always nice to finish top of the times, but we know that doesn’t tell the full story today. The conditions were changing throughout, and we got our lap in when the track was at its driest, while others looked very quick too. We weren’t as competitive in the wet as we were last weekend, so there are a few things for us to understand overnight.

"Tomorrow will be busy if it stays dry and we’ll want to maximise the running ahead of qualifying, particularly to learn about the tyres and any potential graining in these cold conditions. I’m feeling good at the moment though. We’ve been on the front row at the last two races, the performances have been strong, and this is a circuit I really enjoy. Hopefully we can build on that and have another good weekend."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"We saw limited running today due to the conditions and what running we did get in FP2 was on a mix of full Wet and Intermediate tyres. George ended FP2 quickest, but his lap came at the most favourable point when the circuit was at its driest so we’re not getting carried away with the headline position. We struggled to get the tyres working consistently, particularly bringing the front and rear axles into the right window together. With the track evolving almost lap-by-lap it was difficult to get a consistent balance and understand exactly where we stood. That gives us a few things to work through overnight.

"We’re expecting a drier day tomorrow, which means FP3 is going to be very busy. We will use that session to understand the car balance in what we expect to be dry conditions, get a read on the tyres across both single lap and long run work, and assess the level of degradation and whether graining is an issue. That latter point could be particularly important for Saturday given the cooler conditions we are expecting on race day. There’s plenty to get through, but it’s the same challenge for everyone and we’ll look to make the most of the running before qualifying."

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy driving the (12) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Alpine

Alpine came out late, took the flag and thus were the only team to opt for a practice start out there. Franco Colapinto had the biggest moment of the session when he hit a puddle and skewed the rear of his car sideways, fortunately managing to save it before the barriers loomed large.

The team seemed content to wait for the rest to dry the racing line in FP2, coming out late with both cars. But it was their late, late laps that impressed, with Pierre Gasly setting the second-fastest time of the day after the chequered flag fell, winding up just 0.071s behind Russell despite having two big slides on his hot lap.

Pierre Gasly – FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:47.343, P2

“A very challenging day at the wheel with the wet and quite cool conditions. It's always a fun challenge, though, trying to keep the car under control when it's very low grip. We did a couple of laps at the end of Free Practice 1 on the Extreme Wets but there was too much standing water to do anything competitive. While there was no rain during the session, the track was still very damp for Free Practice 2, so we waited for the track to clear up a little before going out on Intermediates. I had quite a good feel in the conditions and just built up the speed bit by bit. In the end, with the track drying, we ended up P2. That's always nice but we are realistic and know the conditions will be very different tomorrow, probably dry, and I am looking forward to having a feel for the car where it's likely to be more representative for what we will see in Qualifying and the Race.”

Franco Colapinto - FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:49.229, P9

“It was a bit of a frustrating day from a driving perspective because, as a driver, you want to get out there and do laps, but we know the conditions were not representative for the rest of the weekend. As the forecast for the rest of the weekend looks dry, there was not really much to learn or the need to take any risks. It was really slippery on track with the surface water, and it was not clearing fast due to the cold temperatures. With the limited running in the dry it will feel almost like a Sprint weekend, with one dry session before Qualifying, so there will likely be a lot of cars on track in Free Practice 3. Hopefully we can be quick and hit the ground running tomorrow and be competitive when it counts in Qualifying.”

Steve Nielsen, Managing Director

“It was very difficult for the drivers out there today with the rain and wet conditions on track. Obviously, it is nice to be up there in P2 on the leaderboard, but we cannot read too much into it given the track evolution at the end of the session. After a difficult couple of races, we always felt this would be a track which might suit the characteristics of our car. We're looking forward to some dry running tomorrow and seeing how the car behaves and we remain quite hopeful after today's performance. We have a few things to assess overnight, even if it might not be representative to the conditions we expect for the rest of the week, but it's a positive start and we look forward to seeing what we can achieve with both cars.”

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Pierre Gasly of France driving the (10) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Franco Colapinto of Argentina driving the (43) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images)

Ferrari

Dino Beganovic did not get much running in Lewis Hamilton’s car, managing just the one lap. Fortunately for Ferrari, the track dried enough for both Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to get lots of running in in the second session.

Leclerc regularly flirted with the top spot on both the full wets and the inters, looking quick throughout the session. Hamilton had a few wobbles in the wet and wound up in sixth, but if tomorrow is dry, it remains to be seen how Ferrari will fare down the long straight here.

Charles Leclerc – FP1 : No time set; FP2: 1:47.605, P3

"A tricky day for all teams across the grid, due to the weather conditions and wet track. There's not much to take away for the rest of the weekend, as it should be dry going forward. We didn't run in FP1, then did quite a few laps in FP2, which was good in terms of what we learned about driving in these conditions. Hopefully some of the takeaways will be beneficial in the future. We will reset tomorrow and see where we stand in FP3."

Lewis Hamilton - FP2: 1:48.483, P6

"There are a couple of good things to take from today. Missing FP1 didn’t cost us too much given the conditions, and it was good to get some running in FP2. We had a few useful findings as the track dried and we transitioned from Wet tyres to Intermediates, which gives us some notes to work from. Tomorrow is expected to be dry, so it will be a different challenge and we’ll need to react quickly during final practice and ahead of qualifying, to put the car in the best possible place."

Dino Beganovic - FP1: No time set

"Due to the rain, the track conditions didn’t allow for much running today. I only put in one installation lap, as was the case for nearly all the other drivers, so we didn’t have the chance to gather any data. It’s still always a pleasure to be back in the SF-26 and I appreciate the opportunity our team has given me today."

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Charles Leclerc of Monaco and Scuderia Ferrari prepares to drive in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Lewis Hamilton of Great Britain driving the (44) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Dino Beganovic of Sweden driving the (38) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 leaves the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Red Bull

Red Bull sent both cars out together for an installation lap in the wet FP1 session, Max Verstappen describing conditions as “like an ice rink.” The Dutchman did not seem any keener to run in FP2, coming out for an installation lap before retreating back to the garage. That is where he remained, while Isack Hadjar ran with the rest and impressed in the tricky conditions.

Verstappen finally came out late on, only to be thwarted by the red flags. When he finally did manage to set his only lap time, the Dutchman complained about a lack of power, telling his Race Engineer it was similar to the issues he encountered in Brazil.

Max Verstappen - FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:50.141, P13

"The conditions weren’t really representative with the weekend looking dry, so there wasn’t much value in running today. We only did a couple of laps to see where the car was at and identify a few areas to focus on tomorrow, but overall it was a pretty unproductive day because of the weather. With only one practice session left before Qualifying, it’s important that we have a good one and optimise everything we can."

Isack Hadjar - FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:48.407, P4

“FP1 was obviously not ideal, we had to wait for the track to dry so it just wasn't worth going out. FP2 was a lot more fun, the conditions improved and we managed to get the mileage we aimed for. There's not too many learnings that we can take from today but tomorrow will be dry, so we'll try and get as much out of that session as possible. I always have a good feeling at this track and I'm excited for tomorrow."

Pierre Wache, Technical Director

"A tricky day today for everyone with the limited running. The conditions were very cold so getting the tyres where we want them is complicated, tomorrow will definitely be a busy day to make up for this evening.

"On Max's side, we didn't plan to run on the Wet tyre which is why we kept Max in the garage. As the track dried we decided to run him on the Inter but the red flag came which gave us even less running for him. He struggled with the car balance, so there is work to do there overnight.

"Isack is quite happy with the car, in these conditions to have a car you trust is important, so that's the main positive from today. It's tricky to predict where we stand at the moment, a lot of teams have brought updates and you couldn't see the full extent of them today, so we'll see where we are tomorrow."

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Max Verstappen of the Netherlands driving the (3) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Isack Hadjar of France driving the (6) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Colin McMaster - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

McLaren

McLaren were one of two teams not to send either car out in FP1, Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri staying dry in the garage instead. They both came out early in FP2 though, and were also the first team to switch to the intermediate tyres. Norris was the more comfortable of the two on that rubber, putting in hot lap after hot lap. He only wound up down the order by dint of completing his laps so much earlier while the racing line was still wet.

As for Piastri, he has a 10-place grid penalty incoming for taking on a new ICE for this weekend.

Lando Norris - FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:48.837, P7

“It’s good to be back on track here in Las Vegas, it’s always an interesting place to drive an F1 car. This is a very low-grip, low-temperature circuit, and that’s only been made more so by the rain today.

“In FP1, the level of rain meant there wasn’t much value in going out, particularly when we expect it to be dry the rest of the weekend, but it was good to get some laps in during FP2, even if the conditions were still damp.

“We’ve got some important work to do tomorrow, particularly on testing some new bits and getting ready for Quali in dry conditions, so FP3 will be important. We’ll do the best we can with the data we’ve gathered today and make sure we’re ready to go tomorrow afternoon.”

Oscar Piastri – FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:48.453, P5

“Overall, a positive session in FP2 after we chose not to run in FP1. With the rain in FP1, it didn’t make much sense to go out as we weren’t going to learn much, the conditions were bad, and we don’t anticipate the rest of the weekend being the same.

“It was useful to get running in FP2 with the new Internal Combustion Engine and turbo so that we could learn as much as we could. It was an interesting and challenging session, with some good learnings on tyre warm-up. The initial few laps on the Inters were tricky, but the car felt much more manageable as the conditions improved towards the end of the session, as a drier line started to appear.

“Looking ahead to tomorrow, while I have a 10-place grid penalty, it doesn’t change our approach to the weekend. We will do what we can to maximise everything ahead of Qualifying and get ourselves up as high up as we can.”

Randy Singh, Senior Director, Racing

“The conditions made it difficult to evaluate the car properly. In the wet, we had to tape up some of the sensors, which meant we could not always get the evidence we wanted, so we decided not to fit the new floor because of the risk and because we did not think we would learn much from it in these conditions.

“We hope to run it tomorrow and assess it more effectively. The rain and standing water made the track challenging, particularly with the walls so close, although the tyres held up well and we were able to do some useful work on the Intermediates as the rain eased. With both sessions wet, there is a lot to get through tomorrow, including preparation for Qualifying, and the programme will be compressed.

“It is clearly impossible to draw conclusions about our pace or likely positions: as usual, we can expect that the top four teams will be very close to each other, and the limited running of today makes it even more difficult to predict what will be the starting grid.”

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Lando Norris of Great Britain and McLaren looks on in the garage prior to practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Oscar Piastri of Australia driving the (81) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

Aston Martin

Zak Crawford was in for Fernando Alonso in FP1 but was not afforded the opportunity to show what he can do thanks to the weather. In the other Aston Martin, Lance Stroll did not head out on track at all in the first session.

Alonso jumped back into the cockpit for FP2 and nearly had the first big moment, sliding towards the barriers and only just stopping before he lost his front wing. After that, he had a better time of it and so did Stroll, those two winding up on the fringes of the top 10.

Fernando Alonso - FP2: 1:49.231, P10

Lance Stroll - FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:49.782, P11

Jak Crawford - FP1: No time set

Alonso says:

"It wasn't very representative today with the wet conditions on track, and we weren't able to learn too much.

"We'll have FP3 to try to learn more about everything, especially on the tyres and degradation in the dry.

"I think getting temperature into the tyres is going to be key tomorrow in these colder conditions, but it's the same for everyone."

Pedro de la Rosa, Team Ambassador

"It was too wet to go out in FP1, and there was not too much to learn in terms of representative data with the rest of the week looking to be dry.

"Unlucky for Jak, as he wasn't able to get any running in during the session. He has been working very hard for this opportunity and he put a lot of hours in in the simulator to be prepared for today."

(Photo by Colin McMaster - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Lance Stroll of Canada driving the (18) Aston Martin F1 Team AMR26 Honda on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images)

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Jak Crawford of United States and Aston Martin F1 Team looks on in the Pitlane during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

Williams

Carlos Sainz has a grid penalty incoming in Las Vegas, after it was revealed he had taken a new turbo in his Williams for the weekend.

The Spaniard had a clean day, as did his team mate even if Alex Albon’s radio message in FP1 gave everyone a clear indication of how difficult the conditions were. He muttered “woah” after sliding through a puddle, but did better in FP2 and was a credible 12th – although whether he can stay there if tomorrow is dry remains to be seen.

Alex Albon - FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:49.829, P12

“The conditions were challenging today, and we didn't get much running in FP1 due to the weather. This track is already tricky with the lowest grip of the year, so there was some sliding around while getting the tyres up to temperature. We are also running the updated turbo this weekend, so we focused on calibrating and setting up our strategy for FP3. The forecast is looking dry tomorrow, however I think we would prefer it to stay wet all weekend, but we'll see what happens."

Carlos Sainz – FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:51.571, P18

“It was a bit of an uneventful day in terms of laps given the wash out in FP1 and the limited running in FP2 after I had to stop early with a small PU issue. We went out on inters in FP2 and whilst this running is less relevant for this weekend, we had some issues in Brazil on that tyre, so I wanted to make sure we had addressed these. I was competitive from the first lap, so that’s a positive from today. The rest of the weekend is dry, so it will a bit of a reset for everyone going into qualifying tomorrow, which should make things interesting."

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Alexander Albon of Thailand driving the (23) Williams FW48 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 19: Carlos Sainz of Spain driving the (55) Williams FW48 Mercedes leaves the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Las Vegas at Las Vegas Strip Circuit on November 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Peter Fox/Getty Images)

Haas

Ryo Hirakawa was in for Ollie Bearman in FP1, but he did not get much running in. Nor did Rafael Camara, who will be desperate for laps as he continues to learn his way around the VF-26. Luckily, the rookie did manage 20 laps in FP2, but the tricky conditions did him no favours and the Brazilian skated wide into he run off area at one point. Bearman was culpable for dawdling on the racing line late on and impeding Hadjar, and was fortunate to be caught out in practice rather than Qualifying.

Bearman also has a grid drop coming after taking a raft of new PU components, and will start from the back of the field on Saturday.

Oliver Bearman - FP2: 1:50.699, P15

“It was definitely a tricky day in Vegas. We started off skipping FP1, but in the end it didn’t really hurt us a lot, as so did everyone in a way. FP2 was challenging to be honest, as we struggled the whole session trying to put temperature into the tyres, even when the track was dry. It was a tough one, but I hope we can learn a lot from it.”

Rafael Camara - FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:53.277, P22

“Overall, we didn’t get a lot of laps in today. We were missing laps from FP1 and going into FP2 with everything new. It was very positive though, even if the rest of the weekend won’t be wet, it’s always good to get more mileage in those conditions to see how the car behaves. Now we can get into the data from FP2 and understand for the future. We need to prepare well for tomorrow, have a clean FP3, and get ready for qualifying.”

Ryo Hirakawa – FP1: No time set

“It was very tricky conditions out there, and it was the right decision from the team. It was challenging but we had to be cautious. Of course, it was a shame for me, but it was also my job to look after the car. I think I’ve run more around this track than I’ve driven, but nonetheless, it’s always a great opportunity when you get behind the wheel of a Formula 1 car, and I thank the team for this weekend.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“It was a tricky Thursday for everyone with the conditions – as this track generally offers low-grip, so when it rains with the low temperature, it’s very slippery and takes a long time to dry up. In FP2, I think we struggled a little bit to get the tyres to work, which we anticipated, but we learned everything we could from these conditions. We’ll now reset and go again tomorrow.”

Racing Bulls

Like McLaren, Racing Bulls did not send either car out in FP1, their drivers opting to stay nice and dry instead. So, they came out early in FP2, running on the wets before switching to the inters. Both Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad completed far fewer laps than most of their rivals, and did not take advantage of the drying racing line late on. As such, they seem a little out of position and would be expected to move up the order tomorrow.

Arvid Lindblad – FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:51.148, P17

"The rain had a significant impact on today’s running and disrupted our plans, meaning we didn’t get as much track time as we would have liked. We managed to complete a few laps in FP2, which were valuable in helping me learn the track and gradually get up to speed. It wasn’t easy, as I think this is probably the lowest-grip circuit on the calendar, especially in these wet conditions and the walls adding another challenge. My focus was on building confidence and getting comfortable with the car, and I felt better towards the end of the session as track conditions started to improve. Let’s see what tomorrow brings."

Liam Lawson - FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:51.009, P16

"Day one in Vegas done. It was very cold and wet out there today, so we weren’t able to get many laps in. The forecast suggests these conditions won’t continue throughout the weekend, but if they do, at least we’ve been able to gather some useful learnings and get a good feel for driving the car. Hopefully, things dry up tomorrow and we can get some proper running in."

Alan Permane, Team Principal

"Quite a strange day here in Las Vegas today. It was wet throughout both sessions, which isn’t what we’re expecting for the remainder of the weekend. We didn’t run in FP1, but in FP2 we completed some laps on the Intermediate tyres to get an idea of where we need to be in terms of cooling levels for the power unit. We’re not reading too much into the lap times, as we’re very much expecting the rest of the weekend to be dry. Because of the two wet sessions today, we’re able to carry an additional set of tyres into FP3 tomorrow. That means we’re expecting a particularly busy session, with all teams likely to use all three sets, so there will be plenty of running and catching up to do!"

Audi

Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto both completed one installation lap in the wet, before returning to the Audi pits.

They ran much more in the second hour of practice, but neither driver could climb up the order on either the wets or the intermediates. Both kept out of the barriers though, and with the pecking order a little unknown, could still impress come tomorrow if the weather turns dry.

Nico Hulkenberg – FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:51.807, P19

“It was a slightly unusual Thursday with the weather playing its part. The rain and standing water limited our running in FP1, but conditions improved for FP2 and we managed to get a decent number of laps in. We gathered some useful information, although it’s still early to draw any real conclusions.

"Tomorrow is still a bit of an unknown, with the weather looking fairly unpredictable. If it stays dry, we’ll be going into qualifying with limited running in those conditions, but that applies to everyone. We’ll need to stay flexible and make the most of whatever we get.”

Gabriel Bortoleto - FP1: No time set; FP2: 1:52.325, P20

“We managed to get a few laps in FP2 after having missed out on FP1 due to the weather conditions. Unfortunately, an issue prevented us from completing the full programme – we opted to wrap up early to properly investigate it and address it, and have it fixed for tomorrow.

“All in all, we only missed around ten minutes of the session, so we still got plenty of mileage in and, overall, I felt quite comfortable in the car. I also had the chance to drive a little in the wet, which was useful. I am feeling quite good and looking forward to FP3 and qualifying tomorrow.”

Pirelli

Simone Berra, Pirelli Chief Engineer

"Today's track conditions limited the teams' workload and made both sessions of little value in preparation for the remainder of the weekend. During FP1, the amount of standing water on the track meant that teams completed only installation laps. In the second session, the circuit gradually evolved from wet to damp, drying very slowly. Full Wets were used in the early stages before teams switched to Intermediates. Neither wet-weather tyre showed any signs of graining, even during the crossover phase.

"As the racing line gradually dried, wear on the Intermediates inevitably increased, particularly in the closing stages of the session when the ideal line was almost completely dry. The switch to slicks never occurred because some areas of the track remained very damp, including the painted road markings, which are especially slippery in these conditions, while the low temperatures would have made it difficult to bring dry-weather tyres up to operating temperature quickly.

"Given that the forecast for both qualifying and the race indicates no risk of rain, the most meaningful work will probably begin tomorrow, when teams will be able to focus on car set-up and gather more useful data to define their strategies. From this perspective, it will be interesting to see which tyre sets are returned at the end of the day, as this could already provide the first indications of the strategic direction teams are taking for the race."

title: F1 set for major V8 engine rule change after agreement finally reached
excerpt:
A return to V8 engines is on the horizon following a key meeting between the FIA and manufacturers.

F1 is to return to V8 engines for the 2030 season after the FIA, FOM, and the F1 power unit manufacturers reached a unanimous agreement on the technical framework.

V8s were last used in F1 in 2013 before the introduction of the 1.6-litre V6 hybrid power units, which started a new era for the sport.

As part of the 2030 regulation shift, the new engines will be a 2.1-litre turbocharged V8 and powered by sustainable fuels.

The FIA has communicated that the main goal of the new power unit is to be less complex, lighter and cheaper than those currently in use.

It is set to scale back on hybridisation and use sustainable technology to generate "attack-orientated racing and a sound which resonates with fans" after many years of complaints regarding the sound of the current power units.

Additionally, the FIA has said that "the plan is to marry the V8 power unit to a chassis which will also be lighter, more agile and place greater emphasis on driver skill and close racing".

Following the agreement, the FIA has detailed that the next step will be to present a definitive 2030 Regulatory Framework to the FIA World Motor Sport Council meeting in Shanghai next month.

[Article continues below]

FIA president hails return of F1 'DNA'

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem hailed the collaboration of all involved and insisted the new direction will bring back the "DNA" of F1.

"This agreement marks a significant milestone in shaping the future of Formula 1," he said.

"From the outset, I have been clear in my ambition to deliver a sport that is more competitive and more exciting for our fans, while remaining at the forefront of innovation and sustainability.

"The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide.

"Our vision is clear: lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition.

"I want to thank all involved for their collaboration. This is an important step forward, and demonstrates what we can achieve when we work together to deliver the best possible future for our sport."

title: Ford Racing announces major leadership change ahead of historic programme
excerpt:
Significant steps taken to drive Ford Racing forward.

Ford Racing has announced two major leadership changes as it prepares for what it calls 'the most ambitious competition schedule in its 125-year history'.

Pascal Zurlinden will join as global director, Ford Racing, from 1 January 2027, taking charge of the entire business, spanning global competition, production vehicles, customer racing and experiences.

Zurlinden, who has held leadership roles at Audi Sport, Porsche Motorsport and most recently Multimatic, will report to Ford chief operating officer Kumar Galhotra.

Mark Rushbrook moves into a dedicated role leading global competition, with Rushbrook and Ford Racing general manager Will Ford reporting to Zurlinden.

"Ford Racing has tremendous momentum, and what we learn on the track makes the vehicles our customers drive better," said Galhotra.

"As the business grows, we need two things: leadership for Ford Racing as a whole, and dedicated leadership for competing at the highest level.

"Pascal brings the technical depth and global experience to take the business forward. Mark built the foundation we're growing from, and there's no one better to lead our global competition programmes as they become more demanding than ever."

Zurlinden eyes 'next chapter'

"As Ford Racing celebrates 125 years, it's an incredible honour to be entrusted with leading Ford Racing into its next chapter and building on the foundation Mark Rushbrook and this team has created," said Zurlinden.

"Ford is creating a vibrant and exciting business around racing, not just on the track but increasingly off track as well. The opportunities ahead are exciting, the team is strong and well prepared, and I'm incredibly proud to take on this challenge together with them."

Rushbrook will focus on a portfolio that includes Red Bull Ford Powertrains in F1, a planned factory return to the World Rally Championship, and a new Hypercar programme joining the World Endurance Championship in 2027 to target outright victory at Le Mans.

"I'm incredibly proud of what this team has built and excited about where we're headed," said Rushbrook.

"Our global competition portfolio has never been stronger or more ambitious. This role allows me to focus on helping our teams and partners compete and win at the highest level. Pascal and I have worked closely together for years, and I'm excited to build on that partnership."

title: Colton Herta has 'decided on a direction' after Cadillac F1 seat snub
excerpt:
Colton Herta will not race for Cadillac next year, but he remains an option for the 2028 campaign.

Cadillac has stated that Colton Herta has “decided on a direction” for his future after he was overlooked for a 2027 promotion to the team.

Earlier this week, the American squad put all speculation to bed when it confirmed Valtteri Bottas would continue for another year in an unchanged line-up alongside Sergio Perez.

title: McLaren missing vital 'evidence' as rain destroys Las Vegas plan
excerpt:
McLaren has explained how the washout conditions in Las Vegas Grand Prix practice means it is missing "evidence" required related to its new upgrades.

A fresh floor, with an eye on 2027, has been delivered for Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, but FP1 in Sin City was a washout due to torrential rain.

Conditions did improve in FP2, with Piastri taking fourth and Norris sixth as the track dried throughout, but the slick tyres were not used throughout the day, with all teams lacking crucial data heading into Friday's on-track action, which will include qualifying.

Reflecting on the tough conditions, racing director Randy Singh explained how the new floor wasn't actually fitted to either MCL40 for fear of damaging it - meaning crucial "evidence" has not been able to be gathered.

"The conditions made it difficult to evaluate the car properly. In the wet, we had to tape up some of the sensors, which meant we could not always get the evidence we wanted, so we decided not to fit the new floor because of the risk and because we did not think we would learn much from it in these conditions," Singh explained.

"We hope to run it tomorrow and assess it more effectively. The rain and standing water made the track challenging, particularly with the walls so close, although the tyres held up well and we were able to do some useful work on the Intermediates as the rain eased.

"With both sessions wet, there is a lot to get through tomorrow, including preparation for Qualifying, and the programme will be compressed."

[Article continues below]

'Impossible conclusions'

Given the ineffective running on Thursday, Singh also declared that it was "impossible" to make any guesses about the pecking order.

"It is clearly impossible to draw conclusions about our pace or likely positions," he said.

"As usual, we can expect that the top four teams will be very close to each other, and the limited running of today makes it even more difficult to predict what will be the starting grid."

title: Lewis Hamilton issues Ferrari demand as Las Vegas GP opportunity beckons
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton is hopeful Ferrari can make the most of limited practice running in dry conditions on Friday in Las Vegas.

Lewis Hamilton has stated Ferrari must "react quickly" to whatever it learns during final practice in Las Vegas after day one's disruption.

Heavy rainfall at the start of FP1 saw teams park the cars in their garages for much of the session, with installation laps being as far as they got.

However, there was more running in FP2, with Hamilton logging 24 laps to place himself in sixth place at the end of the hour.

Friday's weather forecast is set to see dry temperatures, which could make the first day of running largely irrelevant.

When asked if Ferrari is blind heading into qualifying day, Hamilton replied: "Everyone is, really. None of us have put on a set of softs.

"So we'll be faced with challenges. We need to be able to act quickly tomorrow in the practice session, the short hour that we have, and in between the sessions.

"Hopefully it's not bad and we're there or thereabouts."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

British

Ferrari has not yet won at Las Vegas, with Red Bull and Mercedes taking the spoils since the event's inception in 2023.

As Hamilton looks to add to his winning tally this weekend, he stated the sitting around and waiting in the cold conditions reminded him of his early karting days.

"Everyone wants to go racing, everyone wants to be out running," he said.

"It's one of those days, it reminds me of an old day at Rowrah in karting, it's cold and miserable.

"We didn't lose out much missing FP1 because it was so wet. At least we got some running.

"There was a couple of good findings in the session going from the wet to the intermediate.

"It wasn't really a great day, just sitting around waiting. I didn't do much today.

"You can't really test much in those conditions and everything you learn today you have to forget because tomorrow is supposed to be dry.

"So, we kind of start from tomorrow."

title: Terrifying Formula E car explosion concludes pre-season testing
excerpt:
Formula E's 2027 pre-season test has officially concluded, following the final two sessions of the week in Madrid.

Formula E's 2027 pre-season test ended in terrifying fashion, with no running occurring in the final hour after Taylor Barnard's Fusion blew up.

A battery on the Briton's car exploded in the final sector, resulting in a huge fireball that required significant attention from fire crews.

No running in the final hour left Nick Cassidy at the top of the timesheets, but three seconds off the fastest lap of the test.

A mock-'Unleashed' race caught major eyeballs at the start of the afternoon session, with Mahindra's Edoardo Mortara victorious.

Zane Maloney was quickest on Friday morning, posting a 1m 23.838s to become the first driver of the week to dip into the 1m 23s. With Barnard's incident, this ended up as the fastest lap of testing.

Morning session

The opening session on Friday morning – the penultimate of testing – was another hit by red flags, three in total.

Jaguar's Stoffel Vandoorne stopped on the exit of the first corner after leaving the pit lane following a front powertrain issue, a championship-spec part which also forced him to stop on Wednesday.

Two further red flags, taking the weekly total to 15, were caused by Lola's Enzo Fittipaldi, both for going off at the first corner.

The session was topped by Maloney, further improving the young driver's strong start to life with the Japanese manufacturer.

He posted a 1m 23.838s, over two-tenths clear of Envision's Maximilian Günther and Opel's Mitch Evans, who completed the top three.

Afternoon session

The Friday afternoon session – the last of pre-season testing – started with a first-look at the 'Unleashed' race format.

The mock-race was won by Mortara, but also featured Lola's Enzo Fittipaldi stopping halfway through and pulling into the car park.

Normal running returned after the mock race, before the terrifying explosion took place with just an hour remaining. No further running took place.

title: Lando Norris identifies 'important work' for McLaren after Las Vegas curveball
excerpt:
Lando Norris has highlighted that McLaren must improve its understanding of the revised floor it has introduced to the MCL40 at the Las Vegas Grand Prix after rain affected the first two free practice sessions.

Inclement weather saw no one set a timed lap in FP1, and Norris did not even bother venturing out. But once the second hour of running got underway, the Briton looked at ease in the wet- to intermediate-tyre session.

Consistently at the top of the timing board, the McLaren driver was the first to strap on the green-walled Pirellis. Although he ultimately only went eighth-fastest, he decided against putting in a final effort in the closing moments.

Despite that, the MCL40s of Norris and team-mate Oscar Piastri and Charles Leclerc looked the most convincing, even if FP2 ends up being an outlier across the weekend in Sin City.

"It's good to be back on track here in Las Vegas; it's always an interesting place to drive an F1 car," Norris said following FP2 in Nevada.

"This is a very low-grip, low-temperature circuit, and that’s only been made more so by the rain today.

"In FP1, the level of rain meant there wasn't much value in going out, particularly when we expect it to be dry the rest of the weekend, but it was good to get some laps in during FP2, even if the conditions were still damp."

[Article continues below]

McLaren has learning to do

The precarious conditions meant McLaren was unable to fully access the revised floor elements it has brought to Las Vegas, building on the upgrades it successfully delivered in São Paulo.

Therefore, FP3 will be of even more consequence to the papaya team, as it looks to learn more about the potential of its fully updated package.

"We've got some important work to do tomorrow, particularly on testing some new bits and getting ready for Quali in dry conditions, so FP3 will be important," Norris added.

"We'll do the best we can with the data we've gathered today and make sure we’re ready to go tomorrow afternoon."

title: Major F1 rule change handed '100%' verdict despite bizarre stall
excerpt:
Williams boss James Vowles has offered his "100%" backing to the proposed return of V8 engines to F1 - after a bizarre initial announcement.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has been leading the push for grand prix racing to ditch the turbo hybrids in use since 2014 and return to some kind of V8 engines, potentially as soon as 2030.

Earlier this week, a formal announcement was made across FIA channels revealing that it had been agreed by the relevant parties that a 2.1L turbocharged V8 engine of around 900bhp would be introduced - but the announcement was quickly pulled with no formal explanation.

With discussions over the exact framework of the rules still ongoing on the Power Unit Advisory Committee (PUAC), there is no indication of when the announcement will be re-made.

For any rule changes to pass, a supermajority of votes on the PUAC is required - which consists of the five manufacturers - Audi, Ferrari, Honda, Mercedes HPP, and Red Bull Powertrains, the FIA, and Formula 1 management (FOM).

A supermajority requires four of the five PUMs to vote in favour, plus the FIA and FOM, with this vote being a recommendation to the World Motor Sport Council (WMSC) for formal ratification.

Vowles, who is not a member of the PUAC as his Williams team is a Mercedes HPP customer, does not have voting rights, but given his position as a team principal, is involved in wider discussions about the future of grand prix racing.

The idea for the return of the V8s came earlier this year when the new 2026-spec power units were decried by various figures, including world champions Fernando Alonso, Max Verstappen, and Lando Norris, with the new engines featuring a rough 50:50 split in power output between the ICE and newly-beefed up battery systems, capable of producing 350kw of power.

However, once a car depletes its battery power, it begins to slow on the straights to recharge, known as superclipping. The phenomenon was rectified slightly with changes for the Miami GP, and further steps are being made in 2027 and 2028 to increase reliance on the ICE by increasing fuel flow - and thus decreasing dependence on the electrical energy from the batteries.

Offering his take on the return of V8 engines, Vowles gave his full support, with the cars also expected to be considerably lighter for the new era.

"This is a lot of work for something we're changing immediately," Vowles exclusively told RacingNews365.

"But am I completely in support of V8s, smaller hybrid [elements], simpler, cheaper, and lighter cars? 100%.

"The biggest thing we can do is entrench ourselves and say that we have made changes, but I don't think the changes we've made are putting the sport into a better position.

"I think simplification should happen as a result of it.

"I don't think we want V8s where you are deafened by it, but I do think the tone is better, and I do think we can do a better job there.

"It is not so much about that for me; it is about simpler and lighter [cars] because that produces better racing as a result, and hopefully, it'll come back."

title: McLaren explain why it must always 'worry' about Max Verstappen
excerpt:
McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown says his team must always "worry" about Max Verstappen, even when the Red Bull driver starts at the back of the grid.

Brown was asked whether Red Bull's recovery in F1 this season had reminded him of Verstappen's late title challenge last year.

The Milton Keynes-based squad has caught and passed McLaren in the fight for third in the constructors' championship and leads by 17 points with three rounds remaining.

"Chucky. I think that’s the nickname he's been given," Brown told media, including RacingNews365, whilst speaking at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

As Verstappen closed on the McLaren drivers in 2025, the shark from Jaws came up in a podcast interview with Brown, when host Tom Clarkson invoked the film's theme tune.

In Qatar that year, Brown likened Verstappen to a horror villain who keeps coming back. Verstappen supplied the name himself, picking the killer doll from Child's Play.

"He's an unbelievable talent," the American continued. "He's as good as anyone I think we've ever seen in Formula 1. Never really makes mistakes. Tricky conditions seem to play his way, and so look at Brazil again...

"There are a lot of drivers; if they take a penalty or they start at the back, you can go, 'We don't have to worry about them today.'

"But I think when it's Max Verstappen, as long as he's on the racetrack, you need to worry about him."

Power unit penalties left Verstappen P21 on the grid at Interlagos. He reached the top 10 within three laps in the wet and climbed to second as the track dried. Only McLaren's Lando Norris finished ahead of him.

It is the third time in a row Verstappen has come from the rear of the field — or pit lane — to reach the podium in São Paulo.

"He's just an awesome, awesome driver," the McLaren boss added. "It's great to watch him race, and I also like that on his weekends off he still goes in races, so he's a proper racer, and I think he's a talent unlike many we've seen, but not many we've seen before."
